summary: Describes a general architecture for running IPv6 over non-broadcast multiple access networks, where machines cannot simply shout to everyone. It is a proposed standard and was updated by RFC 8064.

plainLanguage.summary: On a network such as ATM, a packet cannot simply be broadcast to everyone on the link. RFC 2491 explains how to make IPv6 work anyway: pretend the network is a shared link, fake the multicast that IPv6 expects, and open a direct virtual circuit to a distant host when there is a lot of traffic between two of them.

what is the ipv6 nbma architecture

subtitle: How to run IPv6 over ATM, Frame Relay and other networks where a packet cannot simply be sent to everyone.

tldr.problem: IPv6 assumes the link under it can multicast, which Ethernet can and an ATM or Frame Relay network cannot. Hosts also expect to reach neighbours directly, which on such a network means setting up a virtual circuit first.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC generalizes the IPv6 link into a Logical Link, emulates multicast with the MARS protocol, and uses NHRP plus Redirect messages to find and open shortcut paths to destinations that are not direct neighbours.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Proposed Standard from January 1999 and was later updated by RFC 8064. It is an architecture: companion documents fill in the details for each NBMA technology.

today: RFC 2491 is a Proposed Standard published in January 1999. It was later updated by RFC 8064; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why NBMA Networks Are Different
sections.content:
Non Broadcast Multiple Access networks can be used in a variety of ways. At one extreme they can provide administratively configurable point to point service, enough to interconnect IPv6 routers and even IPv6 hosts in certain situations. At the other extreme, NBMA networks that support dynamic establishment and teardown of virtual circuits may be used to emulate the service provided to the IPv6 layer by conventional broadcast media such as Ethernet, and that emulation usually requires complex convergence protocols, particularly to support IPv6 multicast.

The document describes a general architecture for IPv6 over NBMA networks and forms the basis for companion documents that provide the details for specific NBMA technologies such as ATM or Frame Relay. It allows conventional host-side operation of the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery protocol while also supporting the establishment of shortcut NBMA forwarding paths when dynamically signaled NBMA links are available, and it describes operations over administratively configured point to point NBMA links as well.

The key difference from earlier IP over NBMA protocols is the mechanism for supporting IPv6 Neighbor Discovery. The IPv4 world used an auxiliary protocol at the link layer, starting with Ethernet ARP, applied to SMDS and ATM. IPv6 developers instead combined several tasks into Neighbor Discovery, which was intended to be non-specific across link layer technologies, on the assumption that the link technology under an IP interface can natively multicast. That assumption is not true of most NBMA services, which usually need convergence protocols to emulate it. This document augments and optimizes the MARS protocol for IPv6 Neighbor Discovery, generalizing its applicability beyond ATM networks.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 was built on the assumption that the network below it behaves like a shared wire where everyone hears everything. Networks like ATM do not work that way, so this document works out how to pretend they do.

sections.title: The Key Components
sections.content:
When the NBMA network is used in PVC mode, each permanent virtual circuit connects exactly two nodes and the use of Neighbor Discovery and other IPv6 features is limited. An IPv6/NBMA interface has only one neighbour on each link. The MARS and NHRP protocols are not necessary, since multicast and broadcast operations collapse down to an NBMA level unicast operation, and dynamically discovered shortcuts are not supported. The details of encapsulations and link token generation are covered by companion documents for each NBMA technology.

When the network is used in SVC mode, the key components are the IPv6 Neighbor model, where neighbours are discovered through messages multicast to members of an IPv6 interface's local IPv6 link; the MARS model, allowing emulation of general multicast using multipoint calls provided by the underlying NBMA network; the NHRP service for seeking out the NBMA identities of IP interfaces that are logically distant at the IP level; and the modelling of IP traffic as flows, optionally using the existence of a flow as the basis for attempting to set up a shortcut link level connection.

In summary, the IPv6 link is generalized to a Logical Link in NBMA environments, analogous to the generalization of the IPv4 IP subnet to a Logical IP Subnet. Interfaces use MARS for general intra-Logical Link multicasting, and the MARS is used to optimally distribute discovery messages within the Logical Link. For destinations that are not currently considered to be neighbours, a host sends the packets to one of its default routers. When appropriately configured, the egress router from a Logical Link is responsible for detecting the existence of an IP packet flow through it that might benefit from a shortcut connection: while continuing to conventionally forward the flow's packets, the router initiates an NHRP query for the flow's destination IP address. The last router, or Next Hop Server, before the target of the NHRP query ascertains the target interface's preferred NBMA address, and the originally querying router then issues a Redirect to the IP source identifying the flow's destination as a transient neighbour.
sections.plainLanguage: Three pieces do the work. MARS fakes the multicast that IPv6 expects. NHRP finds out the network address of a host that is not directly reachable. The routers use both to decide when a direct path is worth opening.

sections.title: Logical Links and Transient Neighbors
sections.content:
IPv6 contains a concept of on-link and off-link. Neighbours are those nodes that are considered on-link and whose link-layer addresses may therefore be located using Neighbor Discovery. An address is on-link if it is covered by one of the link's prefixes, if a neighbouring router specifies the address as the target of a Redirect message, if a Neighbor Advertisement message is received for the target address, or if a Neighbor Discovery message is received from the address. Off-link nodes are considered to be accessible only through one of the routers directly attached to the link.

The NBMA environment complicates the sense of the word link in much the same way it complicated the sense of subnet in the IPv4 case, where a Logical IP Subnet was defined as an administratively constructed set of hosts that would share the same routing prefixes. The IPv6 analog in this document is a Logical Link, which consists of nodes administratively configured to be on link with respect to each other. The members of a Logical Link are an IPv6 interface's initial set of neighbours, and each interface's Link Local address only needs to be unique amongst this set.

While members of a Logical Link are IPv6 neighbours, it is possible for neighbours to exist that are not, administratively, members of the same Logical Link. Neighbor Discovery events can expand an IPv6 interface's set of neighbours without changing the set of interfaces that make up its Logical Link, which leads to three possible relationships between any two IPv6 interfaces: on Logical Link and neighbour, off Logical Link and neighbour, and off Logical Link and not neighbour. Off Logical Link neighbours represent the shortcut connections, where it has been ascertained that direct connectivity at the NBMA level is possible to a target that is not a member of the source's Logical Link. Neighbours discovered through unsolicited messages such as Redirects are termed transient neighbours.
sections.plainLanguage: A Logical Link is the set of machines an administrator has declared to be on the same link. A host may also reach a machine outside that set through a direct connection, and such a machine is called a transient neighbour.

sections.title: Finding Neighbors Inside a Logical Link
sections.content:
The basic model of Neighbor Discovery assumes that a link layer interface will do something meaningful with an ICMPv6 packet sent to a multicast IP destination address. This document assumes multicast support is provided using the MARS service, generalized for use over other NBMA technologies in addition to ATM. An IPv6 Logical Link maps directly onto an IPv6 MARS Cluster in the same way an IPv4 Logical IP Subnet maps onto an IPv4 MARS Cluster. The goal of intra-Logical Link operation is that the IPv6 layer must be able to simply pass multicast ICMPv6 packets down to the IPv6/NBMA driver without any special NBMA specific processing, so that the underlying mechanism for distributing Neighbor Discovery and Router Discovery messages works as expected.

IPv6/NBMA interfaces SHALL register as MARS Cluster members and SHALL send certain classes of outgoing IPv6 packets directly to their local MARS. The MARS then re-transmits these packets by a set of rules. When it receives an IPv6 packet, it scans the group membership database to find the NBMA addresses of the IPv6 destination group's members. It then checks whether every group member currently has its point to point control VC open to the MARS. If so, the MARS sends a copy of the data packet directly to each group member over the existing point to point VCs. If one or more of the discovered group members do not have an open point to point VC to the MARS, or if there are no group members listed, the packet is sent out the ClusterControlVC instead, and no copies are sent over the existing point to point VCs.
sections.plainLanguage: The MARS server stands in for the missing multicast. It looks up who belongs to the group and either sends each of them a copy down the circuits it already has, or passes the packet on to be shared.

sections.title: Redirects and How a Shortcut Is Found
sections.content:
Shortcut connections are justified on the grounds that demanding flows of IP packets may exist between source and destination pairs separated by IP routing boundaries, and shortcuts are created between transient neighbours. The key to creating transient neighbours is the Redirect message. IPv6 allows a router to inform the members of a Logical Link that there is a better first hop to a given destination, and the advertisement is achieved through a Router Redirect message, which may carry the link layer address of this better hop.

A transmitting host only listens to Router Redirects from the router that is currently acting as its default router for the IP destination the Redirect refers to. If a Redirect arrives that indicates a better first hop for a given destination and supplies a link layer address to use as that better first hop, the associated Neighbor Cache entry in the source host is updated and its reachability set to STALE. Updating the cache involves building a new VC to the new NBMA address, and the old VC is torn down only if it is no longer required, since it was to the router and may still be needed by other packets.

Two mechanisms trigger the discovery of a better first hop: router-based flow identification, and a host-initiated shortcut request. For flow triggered redirection, a router MAY choose to initiate the discovery of a better first hop when it determines that an identifiable flow of IP packets is passing through it. Such a router SHALL only track flows that originate from a directly attached host, SHALL NOT use IP packets arriving from another router to trigger the generation of a Router Redirect, and SHALL only consider IPv6 packets with a FlowID of zero for the purposes of flow detection. It SHALL use NHRP to ascertain a better first hop and advertise the information in a Router Redirect. The actual algorithms for deciding what sequence of packets constitutes a flow are outside the scope of the document.

For host triggered redirection, a source host MAY trigger a redirection to a transient neighbour by creating a Neighbor Solicitation message referring to the off-Logical Link destination for which a shortcut is desired and addressing it to the router that would be the next hop for traffic towards that target, rather than to the target's solicited node multicast address. Routers conforming to this document SHALL recognise such Neighbor Solicitation messages as requests for the resolution of off-link addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: A shortcut starts when a router notices a busy flow and looks up the network address of the far end, or when a host asks for one. Either way the router tells the host, in a Redirect, to go straight to that address.

sections.title: Interface Tokens and Link-Local Addresses
sections.content:
Each IPv6 interface must have an interface token from which to form IPv6 autoconfigured addresses. The token must be unique within a Logical Link, to prevent the creation of duplicate addresses when stateless address configuration is used. Where two nodes on the same Logical Link produce the same token, one of them MUST choose another, and all implementations MUST support manual configuration of interface tokens so that operators can change one per Logical Link. All interface tokens MUST be 64 bits in length, and the host tokens are based on the format of an EUI-64 identifier.

Physical NBMA interfaces may be used to provide multiple logical NBMA interfaces, and since each logical interface may support an independent IPv6 interface, two scenarios are possible: a single host with separate IPv6/NBMA interfaces onto a number of independent Logical Links, or a set of two or more virtual hosts sharing a common NBMA driver. In the first case, because each interface is associated with a different Logical Link, the host can reuse a single unique interface token across all of them. In the second case, independent and unique identifiers SHALL be generated for each virtual NBMA interface so that unique interface tokens can be constructed.

Neighbor Discovery defines two option fields for carrying link-layer specific source and target addresses. Between IPv6/NBMA interfaces their format is adapted from the MARS and NHRP specifications and consists of a Type octet, where 1 means source link-layer address and 2 means target link-layer address, a Length octet giving the total length of the option in multiples of 8 octets with zero padding added to reach that, a Number Type and Length octet, a SubAddress Type and Length octet, the NBMA Number and optionally the NBMA Subaddress. The IPv6 link-local address is formed by appending the interface token to the prefix FE80::/64.
sections.plainLanguage: Each interface needs a number that is unique within its Logical Link, and that number becomes the last part of the interface's link-local address, which always begins FE80:.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This architecture introduces no new protocols, but depends on existing protocols, NHRP, IPv6, Neighbor Discovery and MARS, and is therefore subject to all the security threats inherent in those protocols. The architecture should not be used in a domain where any of the base protocols are considered unacceptably insecure. The protocol itself does not introduce additional security threats.

While the proposal introduces no new security mechanisms, all current IPv6 security mechanisms work without modification for NBMA. This includes both authentication and encryption for the Neighbor Discovery protocols as well as for the exchange of IPv6 data packets. The MARS protocol is modified in a manner that does not affect or augment the security offered by RFC 2022.
sections.plainLanguage: The document adds no new security of its own. It inherits whatever security the protocols it builds on already have, so the same warnings apply to IPv6, MARS and NHRP.
